title: Your why
hook: why practice at all? the Talmud says start even for the wrong reason, and Akiva's story shows why (Pesachim 50b)
tomorrow: Ray says Zoe's morning coffee is already a practice. is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: five words. Micah's verdict was three verbs: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Values say what. Today asks why.

People start running for a wedding photo, or go to services to keep a parent happy. Is that cheating? The Talmud has a line that sounds almost backwards. Rav Yehuda, in the name of his teacher Rav, says: a person should always busy himself with Torah and good deeds, even not for their own sake. Even for the wrong reason. Isn't the reason the whole point? Here's the puzzle, and the line's own second half solves it.
screen: `RUNNING FOR A WEDDING PHOTO.` → `EVEN NOT FOR ITS OWN SAKE.` → `ISN'T THE REASON THE POINT?`

segments.voice: Because, the line goes on, out of not for its own sake comes for its own sake. In Hebrew, lishmah: doing the thing for the thing itself, for God and the good, not for praise or reward. Lishmah is the goal. But the rabbis didn't make it the starting line. So you start where you are, and the practice does some of the work on your heart. Tradition tells it about Rabbi Akiva. He was an unlearned shepherd, working for a rich man of Jerusalem, Ben Kalba Savua. His daughter, whom later tradition names Rachel, saw something in him. She said she'd marry him if he went to study Torah. So the man who couldn't read went to the house of study, at least partly for her. Another story says that, before he started, he watched water dripping on a stone until it had worn a hollow, and thought: if soft water can carve stone, words of Torah can carve a heart. He became a great teacher. A beginning that was partly for love of Rachel became a life given to Torah for its own sake. Here's the teaching, plainly: in Jewish tradition you don't wait for a pure motive before you act. You act, and let the doing grow the motive. So write your why honestly, even if it's mixed. Then watch where it goes.
screen: `OUT OF NOT FOR ITS OWN SAKE...` · `...COMES FOR ITS OWN SAKE.` · `AKIVA STARTS FOR RACHEL.` · `WATER CARVES THE STONE.` · then, large: `MY WHY.`

segments.voice: Write one honest line: why practice at all? If the true answer is mixed, to sleep better, to feel less alone, to impress someone, write that. Underneath, leave one blank line for the reason you hope it grows into.
Your why: the honest reason you practice, mixed or not, which the rabbis say can grow into lishmah, for its own sake.
Your line: my why. Akiva started partly for Rachel, and stayed for the Torah. Day 1591, done.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers cite the Talmud's 'from not for its own sake comes for its own sake' to encourage people to begin study and mitzvot before their motives are pure; lishmah, for its own sake, remains the goal.

fork.reveal: Rav says do good even not for its own sake, because that's the road to for its own sake. Lishmah is the goal, not the entry ticket.

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic teaching and debate

Torah.meaning: God's teaching; the Five Books of Moses, and Jewish learning broadly

Rabbi Akiva.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah's era, a shepherd who became a teacher

Ben Kalba Savua.meaning: a wealthy man of Jerusalem, Rachel's father

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 50b (Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for out of not for its own sake comes for its own sake)
Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 62b (Akiva, shepherd of Ben Kalba Savua; his daughter's condition that he go to study)
Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 6 (Akiva and the stone hollowed by dripping water)
